record.card: The testing effect is the finding that recalling studied material can strengthen later retention, rather than merely measure it. Closed-book questions ask learners to retrieve an answer instead of rereading it. Corrective feedback helps when recall fails, making quizzes useful as learning activities as well as assessments.

evidence.locator: Recommendation 5b, printed pp. 21–22
evidence.note: Checked recall-versus-rereading distinction and feedback; retained baseline Testing effect identity instead of creating a duplicate retrieval-practice card.

relations.note: The IES guide discusses retrieval and delayed re-exposure as complementary learning approaches; their mechanisms remain distinct from one another.

record.card: Inattentional blindness is missing a visible event while attention is occupied elsewhere. In the basketball-pass counting demonstration described by OpenStax, many viewers failed to notice an unexpected gorilla-costumed figure. The result concerns divided task demands, not an inability of the eyes to receive the image.

evidence.locator: Selective attention and Simons–Chabris study
evidence.note: OpenStax 5.1 gives the counting task and unexpected figure; many avoids transferring one condition's numerical rate to every observer or task.

record.label: Inattentional blindness
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how a visible unexpected event can escape notice during another task.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly presents the unexpected-figure demonstration as evidence that attention affects perception of the environment; inattentional blindness is the named perceptual failure in that discussion.

concepts.label: Engineering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Prototyping, testing, and revision connect a problem definition with a workable solution.
concepts.card: Engineering turns a practical problem into a design that can be tested. Designers set goals and constraints, build a prototype, compare its behavior with those goals, and revise it. A classroom rover challenge makes this cycle visible.

evidence.locator: Introduce the Challenge, lines 139-142; Criteria for Success and Engineering Constraints, lines 150-165

concepts.label: Go (board game)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Stones share orthogonal liberties, tying local capture to the larger contest for territory.
concepts.card: Go is a two-player board game. Adjacent same-color stones connect horizontally or vertically; liberties are empty intersections beside them in those directions. Diagonals supply neither connection nor liberty. Strings without liberties are captured. Under this guide’s territory scoring, empty territory and prisoners contribute to the score.
concepts.original_description: Exploring territorial strategy and pattern recognition in the game of Go.

concepts.label: Computer science
concepts.learning_takeaway: Algorithms and representations turn inputs into problem-solving outputs.
concepts.card: Computer science studies how information can be represented and processed to solve problems. An algorithm turns inputs into outputs through defined steps. Comparing different procedures for the same task reveals why a correct solution can still be inefficient.

evidence.locator: Computer Science and Problem Solving; Algorithms; Summing Up, lines 199-209, 327-331, 624-633

concepts.label: Gale–Shapley deferred acceptance algorithm
concepts.learning_takeaway: Proposals and provisionally held best offers produce a stable allocation under the specified preference model.
concepts.card: In Gale–Shapley deferred acceptance, each unmatched proposer approaches their best remaining acceptable choice. Recipients hold their best acceptable offer so far, including earlier offers, and reject others. Under fixed strict rankings in the standard one-to-one model, repeating these rounds produces a stable matching.
concepts.original_description: algorithm for solving the stable matching problem

evidence.locator: 2.1 model, PDF p.3, lines 32-46; 2.2 deferred acceptance, PDF p.4, lines 48-66

relations.note: Deferred acceptance solves the stable matching problem.

concepts.label: Testing effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: An initial memory test can strengthen retention on a later test beyond additional study.
concepts.card: The testing effect is improved later retention following an earlier attempt to retrieve studied material. In prose-learning experiments, initial tests could produce better delayed recall than additional reading. Retrieval therefore can serve as a learning event as well as a measure of learning.

evidence.locator: Testing-effect explanation and prose-study example, lines 17-23

relations.note: The authors expressly describe the memory-test intervention as an aid to learning.

concepts.label: Adverse yaw
concepts.learning_takeaway: Unequal drag during an aileron roll can yaw an aircraft opposite to the intended bank.
concepts.card: When an aileron increases lift on one wing, it can also increase that wing’s drag. This differential drag can yaw the aircraft opposite to the intended bank. Adverse yaw therefore couples a roll-control input with an unwanted directional response.

evidence.locator: Chapter 6, Adverse Yaw, printed p. 6-3 / PDF p. 3

relations.note: The aileron section explicitly explains the yaw produced by deflecting these flight-control surfaces.

concepts.label: Airport surface hotspot
concepts.learning_takeaway: Published hotspot locations identify collision or incursion risk that deserves heightened attention.
concepts.card: An FAA airport hotspot is a movement-area location with a history or potential risk of collision or runway incursion. Identifying it directs pilots and vehicle drivers to pay heightened attention there. The designation concerns a risky location rather than a particular incident.

evidence.locator: Hot spot definition, lines 114-117

relations.note: FAA defines this location on an aerodrome movement area as an aviation surface-safety subject.

concepts.label: Boston immediate acceptance mechanism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Finalizing first-choice admissions before later rounds makes preference reporting strategically consequential.
concepts.card: In the Boston school-choice mechanism described in 2003, schools fill seats permanently in rounds of first choices, then second choices and so on. Later applicants cannot displace earlier admissions through higher priority. Consequently, reporting true preferences is not generally a dominant strategy.

evidence.locator: I.A Boston Student Assignment Mechanism, printed pp.732-733 / PDF pp.5-6, lines 362-432

relations.note: The source analyzes the strategy incentives of this allocation mechanism; game theory is an editorial navigation parent.

concepts.label: Bus queue jump
concepts.learning_takeaway: A short bus lane and early green let a transit vehicle bypass waiting traffic at an intersection.
concepts.card: A bus queue jump combines a short lane with a signal arrangement that gives the bus an early green. The bus can pass waiting traffic and rejoin the route ahead of the queue. The treatment links street geometry with signal timing.

evidence.locator: Queue Jumpers, lines 52-54

relations.note: The official passage explicitly defines a short bus lane with signal priority to let buses pass a queue.

concepts.label: Change blindness
concepts.learning_takeaway: An interruption can make a substantial scene change go unnoticed across successive views.
concepts.card: Change blindness is failure to notice a change across successive views of a scene. A brief interruption, such as a blink or blank image, can let a substantial alteration escape detection. The phenomenon exposes limits in comparing scene information over time.

evidence.locator: Opening summary and change-blindness discussion, PDF pp. 1-2, lines 8-18 and 39-45

relations.note: The author expressly discusses this visual-perception phenomenon as evidence about scene representation.

concepts.label: Choice blindness
concepts.learning_takeaway: People can miss a covertly swapped choice outcome and give reasons for the outcome they did not select.
concepts.card: In a choice-blindness experiment, participants selected a face and were sometimes shown the other face as their choice. Some failed to detect the switch and explained the presented outcome. The task reveals a possible gap between choosing and reporting reasons.

evidence.locator: Abstract, PDF pp. 1-2; section 2, PDF p. 4, lines 104-120

relations.note: The paper explicitly studies introspectively derived reports of reasons within the choice-blindness paradigm.

concepts.label: Clarke pivot rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: A VCG payment measures the welfare effect a participant imposes on the other participants.
concepts.card: In a quasilinear VCG mechanism, Clarke pivot payments compare others’ welfare in the chosen allocation with the best welfare they could obtain without that participant. The resulting transfer prices an imposed externality, tying payment to effects on others rather than the participant’s own valuation.

evidence.locator: VCG (with Clarke Pivot Rule), PDF page 7; path-auction example, pages 8-9

relations.note: Editorial parent: the lecture places the rule in the VCG incentive-compatible mechanism framework.

concepts.label: Complex contagion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Some behaviors require reinforcement from multiple contacts, changing how network bridges support their spread.
concepts.card: A complex contagion requires reinforcement from multiple contacts before adoption. In formal network models, an isolated long tie may carry information without supplying enough reinforcement. Several connected contacts can therefore matter for spreading these behaviors through a network.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Introduction, printed pp. 702-703 / PDF pp. 1-2, lines 9-19 and 45-59

relations.note: The authors explicitly distinguish simple and complex social contagions, with complex contagion requiring social affirmation from multiple carriers.

concepts.label: Desirable difficulties
concepts.learning_takeaway: Some practice conditions slow immediate performance while improving later retention or transfer.
concepts.card: Desirable difficulties are learning conditions that can make practice feel harder while improving later retention or transfer. Their value depends on the learner being able to overcome them. Immediate fluency therefore gives an incomplete picture of lasting learning.

evidence.locator: Opening definition, PDF p. 1, lines 1-11; Why Desirable Difficulties Are Desirable, PDF pp. 3-4, lines 60-71

relations.note: The author explicitly frames desirable difficulties as learning conditions affecting retention and transfer.

concepts.label: Duckworth–Lewis–Stern method
concepts.learning_takeaway: DLS revises targets when a limited-overs cricket match is interrupted; the historical Standard Edition models overs and wickets as scoring resources.
concepts.card: The Duckworth–Lewis–Stern method adjusts targets in interrupted limited-overs cricket. ICC uses a Stern Edition calculator; its published Standard Edition fallback explains resources through overs remaining and wickets lost. Edition matters when interpreting the published target-adjustment methodology.

evidence.locator: Duckworth Lewis Stern introduction, lines 9-14
Opening status statement and section 1, PDF p. 1, lines 1-20

relations.note: ICC explicitly describes its adopted DLS method for interrupted cricket matches.

concepts.label: Duration neglect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Remembered evaluations of brief experiences can give duration little weight even when duration is known.
concepts.card: Duration neglect describes evaluations that give an experience’s length little weight even when its duration is known. Fredrickson and Kahneman studied brief affective episodes; remembered evaluations did not simply track elapsed time. Their finding does not automatically extend to experiences lasting months.

evidence.locator: General Discussion, PDF p. 10, lines 1029-1033, 1057-1070

relations.note: The study’s remembered-experience evaluations establish the factual memory connection; memory is an editorial parent.

concepts.label: Dutch roll
concepts.learning_takeaway: Coupled roll and yaw oscillations can have weak damping and may require yaw dampers.
concepts.card: Dutch roll is a coupled oscillation in an aircraft’s rolling and yawing motion. Depending on its lateral and directional stability, the motion may be weakly damped. Some aircraft use a yaw damper to reduce this recurring side-to-side motion.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5, Free Directional Oscillations (Dutch Roll), printed p. 5-20 / PDF p. 20

relations.note: This mode is explicitly taught within the handbook’s Aerodynamics of Flight chapter.

concepts.label: Ephemeron
concepts.learning_takeaway: Conditional retention by a separately reachable key avoids keeping key/value cycles alive.
concepts.card: An ephemeron pairs a key with a value during garbage collection. The value is retained only when the key is reachable without depending on that value. A value’s reference back to its key therefore cannot, by itself, keep the pair alive.

relations.note: Editorial learning parent: Racket’s garbage-collection reachability construct belongs within computer science.

concepts.label: Epoch-based memory reclamation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Epochs and pinned readers delay destruction until no earlier reader can reference retired nodes.
concepts.card: Epoch-based reclamation delays freeing objects removed from a concurrent structure. Readers pin the current epoch while accessing it. Retired objects wait until readers that could still hold references have finished, separating logical removal from safe memory reuse.

evidence.locator: Description; Pinning; Garbage, lines 29-42

relations.note: Epoch-and-pinning reclamation differs from general concurrency and individual hazard pointers.

concepts.label: ETCS braking curve
aliases: European Train Control System braking curve
concepts.learning_takeaway: A train-and-track model predicts speed against distance so ETCS can supervise braking toward a limit.
concepts.card: ETCS braking curves predict how a train’s speed should change with distance toward a restriction. The calculation combines train braking characteristics with track data. These curves support speed supervision; their predicted trajectory is a model, not an exact realized stopping distance.

evidence.locator: Introduction and braking-curve prediction description, lines 15-21

relations.note: The source explicitly describes braking-curve computation as part of ETCS speed-and-position supervision.

concepts.label: Event Segmentation Theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Transient prediction errors mark perceived event boundaries in the proposed account of ongoing activity.
concepts.card: Event Segmentation Theory proposes that people use ongoing models to predict what happens next. A temporary rise in prediction error signals an event boundary and updates processing. The account connects perceived divisions in continuous activity with attention and memory.

evidence.locator: Abstract; A Theory of Event Segmentation, lines 94-113

relations.note: The authors explicitly frame the theory as an account of perceptual boundaries in continuous activity.

concepts.label: Focal closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: A shared activity can help create a friendship.
concepts.card: Focal closure occurs when two people sharing an activity or organization form a social tie. The shared focus supplies a setting for contact. In a social-affiliation network, the resulting edge connects people.

evidence.locator: 4.3, Co-Evolution of Social and Affiliation Networks, PDF p. 12, lines 370-374

relations.note: Shared affiliations can create a social tie.

concepts.label: Friendship paradox
concepts.learning_takeaway: Sampling people through friendship links overrepresents people who have many friends.
concepts.card: The friendship paradox reflects sampling through social ties. People with many friends appear in more people’s friend lists, so they are overrepresented among friends. Average friend counts can consequently be higher in this sample; the statement concerns sampling rather than every individual.

evidence.locator: Abstract, lines 46-48

relations.note: The original abstract explicitly explains comparisons of friend counts in a social network through disproportionate exposure to highly connected friends.

concepts.label: Generation effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Generating a word can improve later memory compared with reading the same word.
concepts.card: Generating a word from a cue can leave a stronger memory than reading it. The generation effect emerged in experiments comparing those encoding conditions, with advantages in later recognition and recall. Its size and occurrence depend on the study conditions.

evidence.locator: Original abstract summary and author retrospective, single PDF page, lines 3-8 and 26-43

relations.note: The author describes the original experiments as comparisons of memory for generated and read words.

concepts.label: Hazard pointer
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reclaim nodes removed from lock-free objects for safe later reuse.
concepts.card: A hazard pointer lets a thread announce that it is protecting an object in concurrent memory. Removed objects are retired before reclamation. Checking published hazard pointers delays freeing protected objects, separating removal from safe reuse of their memory.

evidence.locator: 2 Hazard pointer overview, PDF pp. 4-5, lines 125-162

relations.note: Concurrent computing is broader than this named memory-reclamation methodology.

concepts.label: Homophily
concepts.learning_takeaway: Shared traits often accompany social ties.
concepts.card: Homophily is the tendency for social ties to connect similar people. Shared traits can shape who meets whom and who forms a friendship. It describes a population pattern, allowing many individual ties between unlike people.

evidence.locator: 4.1 Homophily, PDF pp. 2-3, lines 23-45 and 64-78

relations.note: Similarity among connected people in social networks.

concepts.label: HTTP Message Signatures
concepts.learning_takeaway: A signature verifies the chosen covered HTTP components and associated signature metadata.
concepts.card: HTTP Message Signatures authenticate selected request or response components and accompanying signature metadata. The signer builds a defined signature base from those covered parts. Verification therefore concerns the named coverage; it does not automatically authenticate every field or every message byte.

evidence.locator: Abstract; section 3, line 1399; 1.1 Terminology; 7.3.3 Symmetric Cryptography, official text companion lines 254-276 and 3267-3287

relations.note: The RFC applies digital signatures to HTTP signature bases; its symmetric-MAC option lies outside this digital-signature parent.

concepts.label: HTTP structured field dictionary
concepts.learning_takeaway: HTTP field dictionaries map unique textual keys to typed items or inner lists.
concepts.card: An HTTP Structured Fields dictionary is an ordered collection of unique textual keys and typed values. Values may be individual items or inner lists. A field specification gives those keys meaning, letting a common parser handle the representation.

evidence.locator: 3 Structured Data Types, lines 252-259; 3.2 Dictionaries, lines 330-336; 2.4 compatibility, lines 243-246

relations.note: The specification explicitly defines Dictionaries as a top-level representation for HTTP fields.

concepts.label: Illusion of explanatory depth
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trying to explain a mechanism can reveal gaps hidden by an initial feeling of understanding.
concepts.card: The illusion of explanatory depth occurs when a feeling of understanding exceeds one’s ability to explain a mechanism. Attempting a detailed explanation can expose gaps and lower confidence. In the experiments, this gap was especially apparent for explanatory understanding.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Introduction, PDF pp. 1-2, lines 8-17 and 54-65; discussion of recalibration after explanation, PDF p. 15, lines 482-487

relations.note: The authors identify the explanatory-knowledge illusion as a metacognitive problem and test changes in self-ratings of understanding.

concepts.label: Inattentional blindness
concepts.learning_takeaway: Attention to a monitoring task can leave a visible unexpected event unnoticed.
concepts.card: Inattentional blindness occurs when an unexpected visible event escapes awareness while attention is directed elsewhere. In Simons and Chabris’s counting task, some observers missed a conspicuous person crossing the scene. Detection varied with what observers attended to.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Introduction, PDF pp. 1-2, lines 32-56; Procedures and Results, PDF pp. 8-11

relations.note: The original authors explicitly study inattentional blindness as a form of visual perception without focused attention.

concepts.label: Libero in volleyball
concepts.learning_takeaway: A back-row specialist has distinct replacement rights and attacking, blocking and serving limits.
concepts.card: Under FIVB 2025–2028 rules, the Libero replaces back-row players through special replacement procedures. The role cannot serve or block, and cannot complete an attack when the ball is entirely above the net at contact. Defensive specialization therefore comes with defined playing restrictions.

evidence.locator: 19.3.1, printed p. 42 / PDF p. 44; 19.3.2.1-2, printed p. 43 / PDF p. 45

relations.note: FIVB Rule 19 defines the Libero’s role, playing actions and replacements within volleyball.

concepts.label: Unraveling in matching markets
concepts.learning_takeaway: Competition to secure matches can push offers earlier, before useful information becomes available.
concepts.card: In matching-market unraveling, participants arrange appointments progressively earlier to get ahead of competitors. Contracts can be signed before candidates’ qualifications or employers’ needs are clear. Roth and Xing’s historical examples show how this timing race can thin later opportunities.

evidence.locator: Introduction, lines 87-91 and 146-164; I. Unraveling in a prototypical market, lines 177-197

relations.note: Editorial bridge to stable matching: the authors distinguish appointment-date instability from blocking-pair instability and discuss centralized match procedures.

concepts.label: Maximum Score golf
concepts.learning_takeaway: A committee-set cap limits each hole’s stroke score, including holes not finished.
concepts.card: In Maximum Score golf, the committee sets a cap on the score for each hole. A player who does not finish the hole still receives that capped score. The format remains stroke play while bounding the contribution of a difficult hole.

relations.note: Capped stroke totals differ from Stableford points and scoring in sport generally.

concepts.label: McGurk effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Mismatched heard and seen syllables can produce a perceived syllable present in neither input.
concepts.card: The McGurk effect occurs when conflicting heard and seen speech can produce a perceived syllable present in neither input. Auditory ba paired with visual ga can be heard as da. Responses vary across listeners and stimuli, showing variability in audiovisual speech integration.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Introduction, PDF pp. 1-2, lines 8-28 and 63-80

relations.note: The paper characterizes a perceptual speech illusion; perception is a general editorial parent.

concepts.label: Membership closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: An existing friendship can lead to a new affiliation.
concepts.card: Membership closure occurs when someone joins an activity or organization through a friend’s existing affiliation. The added edge connects person and focus. In a social-affiliation network, existing friendships can therefore help shape new memberships.

evidence.locator: 4.3, Co-Evolution of Social and Affiliation Networks, PDF pp. 12-13, lines 375-402

relations.note: Friendship can create a person-to-focus membership edge.

concepts.label: Merkle consistency proof
concepts.learning_takeaway: Intermediate hashes establish that a larger tree preserves an earlier tree’s unchanged prefix.
concepts.card: A Merkle consistency proof connects an earlier tree root to a larger tree root through intermediate hashes. It establishes that the earlier leaves remain an unchanged prefix, supporting append-only history. This checks continuity between trees rather than one leaf’s membership.

relations.note: Append-only prefix preservation differs from leaf membership and general cryptography.

concepts.label: Merkle inclusion proof
concepts.learning_takeaway: An authentication path recomputes a root to establish one leaf’s membership in a tree.
concepts.card: A Merkle inclusion proof supplies the sibling hashes needed to recompute a tree’s root from one leaf. Matching an authenticated root establishes that leaf’s membership under the hash assumptions. It proves inclusion, rather than preservation of the entire earlier tree.

relations.note: One-leaf membership differs from append-only consistency; cryptography is the broad parent.

concepts.label: Moral hazard in teams
concepts.learning_takeaway: Shared observable output with hidden individual actions creates a team-specific free-riding problem.
concepts.card: Moral hazard in teams arises when individual actions are hidden but joint output is observable. In Holmström’s model, sharing that output under a balanced budget can leave members with incentives to free ride. The team setting changes the contract-design problem.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Introduction, printed pp.324-325 / PDF pp.2-3; free-rider discussion, printed p.325 / PDF p.3

relations.note: The introduction explicitly defines the paper’s setting as a multiagent extension of the moral-hazard problem.

concepts.label: Multitask incentive problem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Rewarding measurable output can shift effort away from other valuable duties competing for attention.
concepts.card: A multitask incentive model treats effort as attention allocated across different duties. When duties compete for that attention, rewarding easily measured output can divert effort from valuable work that is harder to measure. The effect depends on task substitution and measurement.

evidence.locator: Introduction, printed pp. 24-26 / PDF pages 1-2, distinguishing mark and competing-attention paragraphs

relations.note: The introduction explicitly contrasts multidimensional principal-agent models with one-dimensional models.

concepts.label: Mutual exclusivity in word learning
concepts.learning_takeaway: An unfamiliar label can be assigned to an unnamed object or property instead of a familiar whole object.
concepts.card: Mutual exclusivity is a word-learning default that discourages assigning an unfamiliar label to an already named whole object. It can guide a learner toward an unnamed object or property. Context can override the assumption; objects may legitimately have multiple names.

evidence.locator: Mutual Exclusivity, printed pp. 140-141 / PDF pp. 4-5; Constraints as Default Assumptions, pp. 142-145

relations.note: The authors explicitly treat mutual exclusivity as a proposed constraint guiding children’s acquisition of word meanings.

concepts.label: Oblivious HTTP
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate relay and gateway split knowledge of client identity and request contents.
concepts.card: Oblivious HTTP sends encrypted requests through a relay to a gateway. The relay sees the client but cannot read the request; the gateway decrypts it but sees the relay. Privacy depends on separated knowledge, including those parties not colluding.

evidence.locator: 2.1 Applicability; section 6, lines 540-550

relations.note: RFC 9458 defines an encrypted relaying mechanism for HTTP requests and responses, a distinct protocol facet.

concepts.label: P-factor
concepts.learning_takeaway: High angle of attack gives propeller blades unequal loading and shifts thrust away from the shaft center.
concepts.card: P-factor is asymmetric propeller loading at a high angle of attack. The blades experience unequal relative airflow, shifting the effective center of thrust away from the shaft. This creates a yawing tendency whose direction depends on propeller rotation.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5, Asymmetric Loading (P-Factor), printed p. 5-32 / PDF p. 32

relations.note: The passage explains the mechanism through the rotating propeller blades and displacement of the thrust center.

concepts.label: Preferential attachment
concepts.learning_takeaway: A node’s existing links can increase its chance of receiving new links, amplifying early differences.
concepts.card: Preferential attachment is a rule in which well-connected nodes are more likely to receive new links. Repeated growth can amplify an initial advantage, producing a few highly connected nodes. This is a simplified network model, not a universal explanation of popularity.

evidence.locator: 18.3 Rich-Get-Richer Models, PDF pp. 5-6, lines 122-156 and 168-171

relations.note: The source provides a network-growth model of link creation; network science is an editorial parent.

concepts.label: Productive failure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Unsuccessful problem exploration can support later transfer when subsequent problems supply a useful contrast.
concepts.card: In Kapur’s 2006 study, student groups initially struggled with ill-structured problems without scaffolding. They later performed better on individual problems, including transfer, than a scaffolded comparison group. The result concerns that staged task design; unsuccessful exploration alone is not a general recipe.

evidence.locator: Abstract, PDF p. 1, lines 4-22; Method/Research Design, printed p. 1588 / PDF p. 2, lines 148-195

relations.note: The experiment explicitly analyzes meaningful learning and transfer after contrasting problem-solving conditions.

concepts.label: QPACK field compression
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate instruction streams let HTTP/3 field compression trade table reuse against blocked decoding.
concepts.card: QPACK compresses HTTP/3 field sections using a shared dynamic table and separate instruction streams. Referring to a table entry that has not arrived can block decoding. Limiting blocked streams trades compression reuse against the cost of waiting.

evidence.locator: Sections 1, 2, 2.1.2

relations.note: RFC 9204 defines QPACK for HTTP/3 field compression, a specific mechanism within HTTP.

concepts.label: Relative performance evaluation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Peers’ outcomes can supply information useful for designing an individual’s incentive contract.
concepts.card: Relative performance evaluation lets a contract use peers’ outcomes alongside an agent’s own performance. In Holmström’s model, comparing agents can provide information useful for incentives. The value of competition therefore depends on its informational role in the contracting problem.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Introduction, printed pp.324-325 / PDF pp.2-3; relative-performance evaluation paragraph, printed p.325 / PDF p.3

relations.note: The abstract and introduction explain how peers’ outcomes inform incentive contracts in the model.

concepts.label: Advantage in rugby union
concepts.learning_takeaway: Play can continue after infringement when the opponents gain clear tactical or territorial advantage.
concepts.card: Rugby union advantage allows play to continue after an infringement when the non-offending team gains clear tactical or territorial benefit. A mere opportunity is insufficient. Subject to the law’s exceptions, the referee can return to the original infringement when no advantage materializes.

evidence.locator: Principle and 7.1-7.3, lines 38-59

relations.note: World Rugby expressly makes advantage a law governing rugby play.

concepts.label: Runway incursion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Incorrect presence on a runway protected area qualifies even without immediate collision consequences.
concepts.card: A runway incursion is an incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person in the protected area of a surface designated for aircraft landing and takeoff. The FAA safety category describes an occurrence, including cases without immediate collision consequences.

evidence.locator: Definition and Category D, lines 115-125

relations.note: Runway is infrastructure; an incursion is a separately defined safety occurrence.

concepts.label: Rural hospitals theorem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Stable matchings cannot change which doctors an undersubscribed hospital hires under strict responsive preferences.
concepts.card: With fixed quotas, strict preferences and responsive hospital rankings, stable hospital–doctor matchings fill the same number of places at each hospital. The rural hospitals theorem also fixes which doctors an undersubscribed hospital receives, even when other assignments change.

evidence.locator: Section 3 fixed responsive hospital quotas, PDF p.7, lines 117-141; section 4 rural hospitals theorem, PDF p.8, lines 143-159

relations.note: Editorial comparison: this theorem concerns a many-to-one extension of the pinned one-to-one stable matching problem; Q620702 is not a taxonomy parent.

concepts.label: Saturation flow rate at a signalized intersection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Continuous-green discharge with no lost time is a reference rate, distinct from actual signal capacity.
concepts.card: Saturation flow rate describes the hourly rate at which a queued lane could discharge under continuous green with no lost time. It is a reference flow: an actual signal cycle allocates only some of its time to effective green.

relations.note: Traffic light is a device; saturation flow is a defined discharge-rate quantity.

concepts.label: Schelling segregation model
concepts.learning_takeaway: Local neighbor preferences in a simplified movement model can create large segregated regions.
concepts.card: In Schelling’s simplified two-group models, people move when local neighbors fail their tolerance threshold. Each move changes nearby composition, potentially prompting further moves and producing clusters. The result illustrates a collective pattern without treating real segregation as a single-cause process.

relations.note: Schelling explicitly models segregation by color.

concepts.label: Simon effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: An irrelevant stimulus location can interfere with a response selected by color or shape.
concepts.card: In a Simon task, a stimulus’s color or shape determines the required response while its location is irrelevant. Responses are often faster when stimulus and response occur on corresponding sides. The Simon effect shows that irrelevant spatial information can influence action selection.

evidence.locator: Instruction, lines 139-146

relations.note: The paper’s experimental response-selection results provide an editorial navigation parent in cognitive psychology.

concepts.label: Stableford scoring
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hole-by-hole points relative to a fixed target determine the winning total.
concepts.card: In Stableford golf, each hole earns points according to the player’s score relative to a fixed target. Those points, rather than the total number of strokes, are added across the round. The player with the most points wins.

relations.note: Score (sport) is broad; Stableford is a distinct named points system.

concepts.label: Start-up lost time at a traffic signal
concepts.learning_takeaway: The first queued vehicles need extra reaction and acceleration time before steady discharge begins.
concepts.card: When a traffic signal turns green, the first queued drivers need time to react and accelerate. Their initially longer discharge headways create start-up lost time before steady flow begins. This reduces the green time available for discharge at the saturation rate.

evidence.locator: 3.1 Queuing and Discharge Characteristics, start-up lost time paragraph, lines 68-77

relations.note: The source defines start-up lost time for a queue starting to discharge after the traffic signal turns green.

concepts.label: Stop-signal reaction time
concepts.learning_takeaway: A race model estimates the hidden latency of stopping from go responses and stop-signal delays.
concepts.card: Stop-signal reaction time estimates the latency of an unobserved stopping process. A race model relates ordinary response times and stop-signal delays to successful stopping. The estimate depends on the model and task behavior; deliberate slowing of go responses can distort interpretation.

evidence.locator: Introduction, lines 174-181; discussion of independence and slowing, lines 477-484

relations.note: The introduction explicitly places stopping and response-inhibition measurement among executive functions.

concepts.label: Tennis service let
concepts.learning_takeaway: A qualifying service let repeats that serve while preserving an earlier service fault.
concepts.card: Under standard ITF rules, a serve that touches the net and is otherwise valid is a service let. That particular serve is repeated. If it was a second serve, an earlier first-service fault remains; the let does not restart the whole service sequence.

evidence.locator: Rule 22 The Let During a Service, printed p.9 / PDF p.12, lines 342-350

relations.note: Rule 22 defines the service let as part of the tennis rules.

concepts.label: Top trading cycles
concepts.learning_takeaway: Directed preference-and-priority cycles assign seats simultaneously and remove completed trades.
concepts.card: In school-choice top trading cycles with strict preference and priority rankings, each remaining student points to their highest-ranked school with seats; each school points to its highest-priority remaining student. Cycles assign seats, remove assigned students, reduce capacities and remove full schools. Repetition completes the allocation.

evidence.locator: I School Choice assumptions, printed p.732 / PDF p.5, lines 309-313; II.B, printed pp.736-737 / PDF pp.9-10, steps 1-k and propositions 3-4, lines 628-710

relations.note: Editorial parent in game theory: the source analyzes strategic reports and allocations in a mechanism-design model.

concepts.label: Voice onset time
concepts.learning_takeaway: Timing between stop release and vocal-fold vibration distinguishes speech sounds.
concepts.card: Voice onset time measures the timing between a stop consonant’s release and the start of vocal-fold vibration. Voicing that begins before release gives a negative value. This timing dimension helps distinguish speech sounds without requiring one universal boundary between phonemes.

evidence.locator: Legacy: Abramson/Lisker VOT Stimuli, definition and synthesized continuum, lines 21-27

relations.note: The laboratory explicitly presents VOT as an acoustic phonetic measure introduced to characterize stop-consonant voicing distinctions.

concepts.label: Volleyball rotational fault
concepts.learning_takeaway: Serving out of rotation is a service-order fault with a correction and specified scoring consequences.
concepts.card: A rotational fault occurs when a volleyball team serves out of order. Under FIVB 2025–2028 rules, the order must be corrected and the opponent receives a point and next serve. The faulty team’s subsequent points are cancelled only if the fault’s start can be determined.

evidence.locator: 7.7 Rotational Fault, printed p. 26 / PDF p. 28

relations.note: The named fault is one of the official game rules for volleyball service order.

concepts.label: Wheelchair tennis two-bounce rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: A wheelchair player may return after two bounces, and the second bounce may fall outside the court.
concepts.card: Wheelchair tennis permits a player to return the ball after a second bounce. The first bounce must still satisfy the ordinary court-boundary rule; the second may land outside the court. The adaptation changes return timing while preserving the first-bounce requirement.

evidence.locator: Rules of Wheelchair Tennis a. The Two Bounce Rule, printed p.16 / PDF p.19, lines 565-571; ordinary boundary Rules 24(c)-25, printed pp.10-11 / PDF pp.13-14, lines 363-364 and 414-430

relations.note: The Rules of Wheelchair Tennis explicitly introduce exceptions to the ITF Rules of Tennis.

concepts.label: Whole-object assumption in word learning
concepts.learning_takeaway: A new object label is initially interpreted as naming the whole object rather than its parts or material.
concepts.card: The whole-object assumption is an initial hypothesis in word learning: a new label for an object names the object as a whole. It narrows possible meanings among parts, substances and properties, but other linguistic and contextual cues can override it.

evidence.locator: The Taxonomic and Whole Object Assumptions, printed p. 139 / PDF p. 3, lines 79-85; default-bias qualification, p. 145 / PDF p. 9, lines 274-299

relations.note: The paper explicitly defines it as one of the biases used by children to constrain possible meanings during word learning.

issues.note: This mechanism-focused shard has 1 named subject, the existing Go board game, and 0 new named subjects. Eponymous algorithms, theories and scoring methods remain ideas; the global named-subject goal is a soft measured goal.

Some preferred NACTO, Pressbooks, eLife/PMC and Nobel pages returned access errors or client challenges. Inspected FTA, Haskins/author papers, PLOS and Roth-Xing author HTML provide the selected support. Search snippets and the saved stop-signal client-challenge page are excluded as explanatory evidence.

Hazard-pointer protection and deferred reclamation were inspected in P2530R3. The friendship-paradox card stays within primary-abstract support. Relative-performance support now includes the inspected primary introduction. Edition-specific DLS mechanics remain qualified.
